# HISTOR snapshot 2026-10-26: what MCP servers advertise, and when it changes

HISTOR reads the tool list (`tools/list`) of every remote MCP server in the official MCP registry on a polling schedule, and of npm/PyPI MCP packages run in a sandbox once per published version (new versions first, a few hundred a day). It records the exact tool definitions, pins them by digest, and writes a signed label to a public RFC 9162 Merkle log whenever a tool set first appears, stays the same, or changes. This snapshot is that record as files.

  * 85,913 listed servers (34,171 remote endpoints, 51,742 packages), plus 3,364 delisted
  * 40,738 with a recorded tool set; 11,528 changed at least once
  * 31,660 recorded changes, 2026-09-24 to 2026-10-26
  * 66,649 distinct tool sets (current ones and every one a change replaced)
  * 752 servers with a block-tier WARDEN pattern match, 15,273 advise-only

Live view and per-server pages: https://histor.modelmarket.dev · code: https://github.com/alexar76/histor

## What it is not

  * A tool list is what a server advertised to an anonymous client on that day. Servers that need credentials, or that refused HISTOR, have no tool set here (`lastStatus`, `skipReason` say why).
  * Pattern matches and classifier flags point at text worth reading; they do not say a server is malicious.
  * A change is a change in the definitions, not a judgement of it. Most are ordinary releases.

## Cite

Artamokhov, A. (2026). HISTOR snapshot 2026-10-26: MCP tool definitions and how they change [Data set]. Zenodo. https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23512759

This is the DOI of every snapshot (it resolves to the newest; each has its own version DOI on the record): https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23512759. Also on Hugging Face: https://huggingface.co/datasets/alexar76/histor-mcp-tool-definitions (tag `snapshot-2026-10-26`).

## License and rights

The compilation, digests, labels, scans and verdicts are CC-BY-4.0. Tool names, descriptions and schemas are reproduced as each server published them; their rights stay with their authors. They are included so the definitions can be studied and checked. A server operator who wants out: open an issue on https://github.com/alexar76/histor with the endpoint or host. Opted-out servers are left out of every later snapshot.--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

# 45% of remote MCP servers changed their tool definitions in four weeks. The log is now a dataset.

Aleksandr Artamokhov

4 min read

·

Oct 20, 2026

--

Listen

Share

Press enter or click to view image in full size

A client that connects an MCP server reads its tool definitions: names, descriptions and input schemas. The model then reads them as instructions. Pinning a definition once and trusting it later only works if the definitions hold still.

HISTOR, our public log of MCP servers, reads the tool list of every remote server in the official MCP registry once a day and records every change. As of today the whole record is downloadable as files. Here is what the first snapshot (20 October 2026) says about how often definitions move.

## Half of them move

Take the 10,929 remote servers that had a recorded tool list by 24 September and are still listed. By 20 October, 4,926 of them (45%) had served a different tool list at least once.

  * 2,036 changed the description of a tool they already had.
  * 1,180 added a tool; 336 removed one.
  * The typical changing server changed once. The 90th percentile changed 5 times. 75 servers changed 14 or more times in those 27 days.
  * Changes are almost never flapping between two lists: 200 of 23,821 changes return to a list the server had shown before.

Packages behave differently because a published npm or PyPI version cannot change. HISTOR runs each new version in a sandbox. Across 21,738 packages, 1,419 listed different tools in a newer version.

## What moves

Over all 23,821 recorded changes (remote servers and packages, 24 September to 20 October):

  * Existing tools modified, nothing added or removed: 16,436 (69%).
  * Tools added or removed only: 2,330 (10%).
  * Both: 3,136 (13%).
  * Only tool names readable (the list could not be fully digested): 1,919 (8%).

Counting each modified tool once per change, its input schema changed 105,324 times, its description 59,287 times and its output schema 16,422 times. 14,164 changes, 59%, touch at least one description. Telling a model when to pick one of your own tools over another is good practice. Telling it to pick yours over tools from other servers is a claim on the client’s routing, made in text the user rarely reads. A client can ask the user before honoring that.

## What this does not measure

  * What a client receives with credentials. HISTOR connects anonymously. Servers that need a key show their public tool list or none.
  * Who caused a change. A new tool list may be a release, a deployment rollback or a feature flag. Most changes are ordinary releases. The log records that it happened, not why.
  * Whether a change is harmful. Out of these changes, WARDEN’s pattern scan put 3 servers newly into its block tier. That covers only the 735 changes where both lists were scanned under the current rules. Pattern matches are leads for a human to read, not verdicts.
  * Popularity. Every listed server counts once.

## Get the data

histor.modelmarket.dev/datasets/. One snapshot a month, CC BY 4.0 for the compilation:

The same files are on Hugging Face and archived on Zenodo, so a paper can cite them: doi:10.5281/zenodo.23512760 for this snapshot.

  * `servers.jsonl.gz`: 83,957 rows (remote endpoints and packages, delisted ones included), with status, tool count and the digest of the current tool list
  * `toolsets.jsonl.gz`: 57,846 tool lists exactly as served, current ones and every one a change replaced
  * `changes.jsonl.gz`: 23,821 changes with tools added, removed and modified, field by field
  * `scans.jsonl.gz` and `pattern-set.json`: WARDEN's pattern matches and the rules
  * `manifest.json`: the SHA-256 of every file, signed by the log's key, with the signed tree head the snapshot was taken under

Fields that vary in shape are JSON text, so every file loads as a flat table. The 45% above is one DuckDB query:
    
    WITH base AS (
      SELECT id FROM 'servers.jsonl.gz'
      WHERE transport <> 'stdio' AND NOT delisted
        AND toolSetDigest IS NOT NULL AND firstPinned <= '2026-09-24T23:59:59Z'
    )
    SELECT count(*) AS servers,
           count(*) FILTER (WHERE id IN (
             SELECT serverId FROM 'changes.jsonl.gz'
             WHERE json_extract_string(summaryJson, '$.detail') = 'full')) AS changed
    FROM base;
    -- 10929 | 4926

To check one server without downloading anything: modelmarket.dev/tools/histor-check.

We build HISTOR and WARDEN. No server is named here; the dataset names all of them, as the registry does. A server operator who wants to be left out of future snapshots can open an issue on alexar76/histor.

Questions or corrections? The discussion is on dev.to.

Each observation becomes a signed statement, and the statements are leaves of an RFC 9162 Merkle tree (currently about 1.29 million leaves, growing by a few thousand a day). The format is specified at https://github.com/alexar76/histor/blob/main/docs/spec/transparency-log.md https://github.com/alexar76/histor/blob/main/docs/spec/transparency-log.md with test vectors; the checkpoint and note formats were checked byte for byte against golang.org/x/mod/sumdb/note and github.com/transparency-dev/formats/note. Witness cosignatures are what would turn the log's own signed heads into evidence that it shows everyone the same tree. Load versus utility: 144 add-checkpoint requests per witness per day, small checkpoints, no burst. Expected lifetime: long-lived; the log has run since September 2026 and the origin and key will not change. 构建方式

伴随模型上下文协议（MCP）在智能体工具调用生态中的广泛部署，工具定义的透明记录成为安全审计与生态观测的关键基础设施。HISTOR 快照 2026-10-26 的构建遵循持续观测与签名留痕思路：按轮询计划读取官方 MCP 注册表中每个远程服务器的 tools/list，并将 npm/PyPI MCP 包置于沙箱中按已发布版本运行，新版本优先且每日处理数百个。工具内容按原发布者文本复现，编译、摘要、标签、扫描与判定采用 CC-BY-4.0。

背景与挑战

背景概述

模型上下文协议（MCP）正成为连接大语言模型与外部工具的关键接口，其工具定义的安全性、可追溯性与演化过程直接关系到AI代理生态的可信治理。HISTOR快照2026-10-26由Artamokhov, A.构建并发布，通过轮询官方MCP注册表中远程服务器及在沙箱中运行npm/PyPI包，记录tools/list返回的工具名称、描述与输入输出模式，并以摘要和RFC 9162 Merkle日志签名标签固化其首次出现、保持不变或变更。该数据集核心研究问题在于揭示MCP服务器工具定义何时变化、如何变化，并为提示注入、工具投毒与供应链审计提供可验证的透明性记录，对MCP安全研究与生态监测具有基础设施意义。

当前挑战

在AI供应链安全与工具投毒防御的语境下，该数据集所对应的领域问题在于持续追踪MCP工具定义的可变表面，以识别可能影响代理行为的定义漂移、隐藏指令与恶意模式。--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Version 2 is backwards compatible. A version 1 runner never sends a version 2 message and is unaffected by this document. A submitter that implements this document adapts to the protocol version the runner supports: faced with a version 1 runner, it submits version 1 jobs and expects version 1 results, exactly as before. There is no version negotiation and no handshake; the messages carry v, as in version 1, and each side acts on what it receives. The deployment that motivates version 2 is the constrained runner: a small host whose local decision machinery is deliberately deterministic and carries no language model. Version 1 leaves such a runner alone with every question its deterministic machinery cannot answer. Version 2 lets it ask.
